Field studies of the Short Blind Dart Skink (Typhlacontias brevipes) have provided detailed insights into its early development. Eggs incubated under controlled laboratory conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] hatch after approximately 100 days [ab = approximately 100 days], a developmental period that is notably extended compared to many other species within the Scincidae family. Newly emerged neonates are strikingly small, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo within the relatively small leathery-shelled egg. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on these endogenous nutrients during the first days post-hatching, and the subsequent onset of exogenous feeding marks a critical transition. Hatchlings begin to forage for tiny arthropods soon after absorption of the residual yolk is complete, initiating a period of rapid growth that will carry them toward the sub-adult stage.

The reproductive biology of Typhlacontias brevipes reveals a conservative strategy typical of many fossorial skinks. Females produce a single litter per season [F_R_i = single litter per season], and each litter contains exactly 3 young [N_R_i = each litter contains exactly 3 young]. This maximum reproductive rate is observed when environmental temperatures are stable at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The combination of small litter size and infrequent reproductive events suggests that females invest considerable resources into each individual offspring, a hypothesis supported by the relatively large size of neonates at birth. Gravid individuals are rarely observed above ground, indicating that most reproductive activity occurs within the subterranean burrow systems that this species inhabits. The timing of parturition appears to be synchronized with the rainy season, when soil moisture and prey availability are at their peak, ensuring optimal conditions for the survival of the altricial hatchlings.

Respiratory physiology data place the Short Blind Dart Skink among the most metabolically conservative of the scincid lizards. Respirometry trials conducted at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] recorded a maximum basal metabolic rate of 0.0003 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 0.0003 milliliters of oxygen per minute]. This extremely low oxygen consumption rate is consistent with a sedentary, fossorial lifestyle that minimizes energy expenditure. The mass-specific metabolic rate, when calculated against the species' ultimate wet weight, underscores the low energetic demands of adult individuals. Basal maintenance requirements are correspondingly modest, allowing this species to thrive in environments where food resources are patchily distributed. The thermal sensitivity of metabolic rate in this species has not been fully characterized, but the single measurement at 15 °C provides a valuable baseline for future comparative studies with related scincids that occupy similar ecological niches.

Adult body size in this species is modest, with individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 55.18 grams [Wwi = 55.18 grams]. This asymptotic mass is attained after a prolonged growth phase that extends well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity. The maximum lifespan of the Short Blind Dart Skink is estimated at 4 years [am = 4 years], based on extrapolations from long-term field observations of the congener Chalcides chalcides at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], this lifespan is comparable to that of other small, burrowing skinks from arid and semi-arid regions. The trade-off between longevity and reproductive output appears to be finely balanced, as the annual reproductive effort is relatively low. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in body condition and a reduction in locomotor performance, which may increase vulnerability to predation from snakes and birds of prey.

Sexual maturation in female Short Blind Dart Skinks occurs after a defined period of juvenile growth. The time following metamorphosis at which females attain puberty is 365 days [tp = 365 days], a duration measured under thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively long pre-reproductive period allows females to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support both gestation and the subsequent nutritional demands of the 3 young they will produce. Puberty is marked by the onset of gametogenesis and the first detectable vitellogenic activity in the ovaries. The synchronization of reproductive maturation with seasonal environmental cues, likely photoperiod and soil temperature, ensures that first reproduction coincides with periods of maximum resource availability. Post-pubertal females exhibit a consistent pattern of annual reproduction, with most individuals successfully producing a single litter each season until they reach the end of their 4-year lifespan (4 years) [am = 4 years] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
